query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A graded refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer with a tailored composition that provides an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and robust diffusion barrier properties will mitigate thermal stresses and interdiffusion between tungsten (W) and CuCrZr under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A direct interface between tungsten and CuCrZr, characterized by significant differences in thermo‐mechanical properties and prone to high interfacial stresses and unwanted interdiffusion.
generation.intervention: Introduce a graded interlayer fabricated from a refractory HEA, engineered via advanced processing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) to gradually transition the properties between W and CuCrZr.
generation.conditions: High heat flux, elevated operating temperatures, and irradiation conditions typical of nuclear fusion reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The compositionally graded microstructure of the refractory HEA interlayer, which gradually adapts the thermal expansion coefficient and acts as a physical and chemical diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: By providing a smooth gradient in thermo‐mechanical properties, the HEA interlayer reduces the mismatch in thermal expansion between tungsten and CuCrZr, thereby lowering induced interfacial stresses and preventing deleterious interdiffusion and reaction.
generation.predicted_outcome: The incorporation of the graded HEA interlayer will result in improved interfacial bonding, reduced thermal stress accumulation, and minimized interdiffusion, enhancing the overall durability and performance of the joint under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.baseline: Direct bonding of tungsten to CuCrZr typically leads to significant thermal stresses and interdiffusion, which compromise joint integrity under extreme operating conditions.
generation.boundary: The expected improvements depend on the precise optimization of the HEA composition and processing parameters; insufficient control could negate the benefits of the graded transition, and long-term radiation effects remain to be fully characterized.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal compositional range for the graded HEA interlayer and its long-term stability under extreme irradiation and thermal cycles require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of W/graded-HEA/CuCrZr joints with varying HEA interlayer compositions. Expose these samples to simulated fusion reactor conditions including high heat flux, elevated temperatures, and controlled irradiation. Compare the performance metrics against control samples with direct W-CuCrZr bonding.
measurements: Residual stress measurement using X-ray diffraction
Interdiffusion profiling and interfacial chemistry analysis via electron microscopy and EDS
Mechanical strength and durability testing under thermal cycling and irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If joints incorporating the graded HEA interlayer do not show a statistically significant reduction in residual stresses and interdiffusion, along with improved mechanical performance relative to the direct bond baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

In this paper, the impact of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) on the phase evolution and mechanical properties development of CoCrFeNiTi high–entropy alloys (HEAs) was investigated. The microstructure and properties of the material were examined, using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for surface morphology observation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis, and hardness testing to evaluate mechanical performance. The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases. Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa. frame.system: A joined system of tungsten (W) and a copper alloy (CuCrZr) used in a nuclear fusion environment, where the materials are subjected to high thermal loads, irradiation, and extreme environmental conditions.
frame.goal: To identify an interlayer material that can effectively bond W and CuCrZr while accommodating their large differences in thermo‐mechanical properties and protecting against interdiffusion and degradation under fusion reactor conditions.
frame.limitation: Direct joining of W to CuCrZr is challenging due to mismatches in thermal expansion coefficients, thermal conductivities, and potential issues with diffusion and reaction at the interface.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys targeted extreme environments by developing tungsten‐based and related alloys with single‐phase BCC structures that offer high irradiation resistance and thermal stability. Researchers then shifted to advanced processing routes such as laser cladding and laser powder bed fusion to produce coatings and bulk materials with finer, controlled microstructures and improved oxidation resistance. Although these studies achieved notable improvements in high‐temperature mechanical properties, they did not directly address the tougher challenge of joining dissimilar materials with significant thermo‐mechanical mismatches.
decision.unsolved: A direct, reliable joining method for tungsten and CuCrZr under fusion reactor conditions remains unaddressed. In particular, there is a need for an interlayer that can accommodate the large differences in thermal expansion, manage high heat flux and irradiation, and act as an effective diffusion barrier to prevent interdiffusion or deleterious reactions.
decision.lever: fabrication of a graded interlayer based on a refractory high‐entropy alloy whose composition is engineered to provide an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and inherent diffusion barrier properties
decision.why: Building on the trend of using advanced processing techniques to control microstructure and interface chemistry, a graded or compositionally tailored interlayer leveraging refractory HEA technology is the most plausible next step. Such an approach would directly address the thermal expansion mismatch and interdiffusion issues by smoothing the transition between tungsten and CuCrZr, ensuring robust performance under the severe conditions of a fusion reactor.
